Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions

a b s t r a c t
Transition metal (TM) catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are the utmost versatile and reliable methods
for the production of many industrially important fine chemicals. The utilization of transition metals
nanocatalysts in organic transformations, specifically the Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira cross-coupling
reactions, have enticed the vigilant eye of researchers and technologists due to; (i) high surface area,
(ii) higher number of surface atoms leading to large number of catalytic active centers, and (iii) chemical
stability. Moreover, being colloidal, nanomaterials combine the properties of both homogeneous and
heterogeneous. i.e., solubility in different solvents and ease in the separation of catalysts. This improves
the overall catalytic efficiency and cost. Therefore, these pseudo-homogeneous nanocatalysts are gaining
a great deal of attention due to their broad substrate scope and ease of handling. This review article
focuses on the recent advances in developing nanostructured catalysts and their utilization for selective
carbon–carbon bond-forming reactions, e.g., Suzuki, Heck, and Sonogashira coupling reactions. The main
focus is laid on the reactions catalyzed by nanocatalysts derived from transition metals such as Pd, Pt, Cu,
Ag, Ni, Fe, Au, and Zn, expounding the conception and rationale based on the reactivity improvement and
the recyclability of the nanocatalysts are presented here. The heterogeneous catalysis, essential in daily
chemical transformations, is demonstrated, implicating significant functions presented by the nanocata-
lysts, related pros and cons, recyclability, and efficiency.

1. Introduction
TM-catalyzed cross-coupling reactions are amongst the most
powerful tools that find widespread applications in synthesizing
natural products, functional materials, pharmaceuticals, and agro-
chemicals [1,2]. Among them, Suzuki-Miyaura (Suzuki), Mizoroki-
Heck (Heck), and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions are consid-
ered the most versatile and broadly applied reactions for the for-
mation of C<sub>A</sub>C, C@C, and C„C, respectively [3,4] (Scheme 1).
These three reactions have significant practical and theoretical
significance in pharmaceuticals, polymers, and natural product
synthesis. These reactions are also used for the intra-cellular syn-
thesis of therapeutic molecules [5]. Traditionally, these reactions
are catalyzed by homogeneous Pd-complexed catalysts and ligands
such as phosphor and N-heterocyclic carbene [6–8]. Despite signif
icant advancements in attaining higher activity, enhanced selectiv-
ity, and broader substrate scope, homogeneous Pd catalysts suffer
from liabilities such as toxicity and post-processing procurement
of most of the ligands used, expensive downstream separation
[9] of residual metal from the final product below the maximum
allowable level, and reusability of the catalyst [10]. Moreover, the
use of toxic solvents, cumbersome multi-step synthesis involved
in their preparation, tedious handling due to their air sensitivity,
and laborious chromatographic purification of the product also
pose a challenge. Consequently, homogeneous Pd catalysts are far
from industrial realism [11,12].
Recently, heterogeneous metal catalysis has been gaining much
attention due to its superior catalytic activity, broad substrate
scope, and ease of handling [13]. The nanocatalysts are easy to
recover by filtration or centrifugation, allowing reusability of the
catalyst after the completion of the reactions [3,14,15]. A great part
of the former heterogenous catalysis community is emerging into
the nanoparticle community, as highlighted in the special issue
of the prestigious journal ‘‘Chem. Rev.”(nanocatalysts) [16]. More-
over, nanocatalysts-based transformation is considered a non-
hazardous and greener approach, which is desirable for sustain-
ability and economic viability [17]. In addition, nanocatalysts that
are built up on TM nanoparticles (NPs) such as Au, Cu, Pd, and their
alloys can drive a wide range of C C cross-coupling reactions and
C-Het (N, S, N) bond formations with enhanced catalytic activity,
broad substrate scope, and improved yields [15]. These catalyst
systems are generally free from ligands and the requirement of
air and moisture-sensitive conditions [15]. Materials in the nano-
size regime bear the highest surface area and the highest number
of surface atoms that can be further tuned through the synthesis
method employed. This leads to higher catalytic efficiency due
to; (i) increasing the contact between the substrate and catalytic
center, (ii) offering many catalytic active sites per unit volume as
compared to bulk heterogeneous counterpart, (iii) higher zeta
potential values, and (iv) due to unique surface chemistry associ-
ated with the nanomaterials [18,19].
Consequently, TM NPs based nanocatalysts have emerged as
promising alternatives to conventional homogeneous complexes
and demonstrated a plethora of applications in medicinal chem-
istry, electronics, and industrial settings [20–23]. In particular,
the application of TM NPs based nanocatalysts in Suzuki, Heck,
and Sonogashira cross-coupling reactions has witnessed phenome-
nal growth in the past decade. For instance, a search on Scopus for
articles published since 2010 on the subject matter described in
this review is illustrated in Fig. 1.
The data show that in recent years, there has been remarkable
growth in the utility of nanocatalysts for coupling reactions. How-
ever, issues of their low selectivity, the requirement of harsher
reaction conditions, leaching of metal species from the support,
and side product formation need to be addressed [24]. Likewise,
the controversy of whether it is the surface of NPs (heterogeneous
pathway) or the leached metal species in the solution
(homogeneous pathway) involved in the catalysis process also
requires further attention. As a result, searching for efficient

2. The design of nanocatalysts
The nanocatalysts catalytic efficiency, selectivity, and recycla-
bility depend on the nanoparticles’ size, shape, composition, and
assembly, and their instauration with the support. Nanocatalysts
may be deigned as nanocrystals, clusters of metals, metals oxide,
and nonoxides of various sizes and shapes. These may involve no
support materials or may be supported on carbonaceous materials,
polymers, metal oxide, or porous materials such as siliceous
mesocellular foam [50]. The rational design of nanocatalysts is
important to achieve enhanced catalytic activity, chemical and
thermal stability, selectivity, and high efficiency [51]. The tailored
nanomaterials would necessitate tuning their chemical and physi
cal properties as efficient nanocatalysts through particle size,
shape, surface composition, and surface reactivity [52]. It is widely
known that electron transfer occurs between the catalyst surface
and the reactive species in all key steps of the catalytic reactions,
including the reactants adsorption, intermediates diffusion, and
the desorption of the products [53]. Thus, tuning the spatial and
energy distribution of valence electrons at the catalyst surface
would enhance the catalytic efficiency, such as the activation
energy barrier, which in turn is linked to the reactivity and selec-
tivity of the catalysts [54,55]. Based on frontier molecular orbital
theory, adsorption and bonding of reactants on the surface of the
catalyst are dependent upon matching their energy levels to those
of the catalyst surfaces as well as the symmetry and spin state of
the reactant’s molecular or atomic orbitals [56,57]. These proper-
ties of nanomaterials can be achieved/tuned by altering their size,
lattice framework, morphology, quantum size, and electronic
effects from nanopore confinement [58–65]. Likewise, the sup-
port’s size, shape, and composition are critically important in the
design of catalysts [62,63]. In addition, nanocatalysts’ thermal
and chemical stability is also very important since catalysts can
be deactivated because of surface aggregation, leaching, phase
changes, and sintering [64,65].
2.1. Size effect
One of the foremost importance of using nanocatalysts is their
small size because this is directly linked with other parameters
such as high surface area, chemical stability, and reactivity respon-
sible for the enhanced catalytic activities. Therefore, in the past
year, enormous work has been dedicated to nanosized catalysts
to understand the effect of particle size on their catalytic and elec-
tronic properties in numerous transformations, more specifically,
coupling reactions [66,67]. When the size of the NPs decreases,
the ratio of surface to the bulk atoms increases, denoting that more
surface atoms eventually be accessible for the reactions. However,
catalytic activity is not often in direct proportion with the
increased surface area of smaller NPs [68]. The surface of nanocat-
alysts with assorted facets can offer diverse binding force strength
and configuration, which prolong different active sites, steps, and
corners of surface terraces. Therefore, the size and shape of the
NPs significantly affect their catalytic performance [69–76]. Like-
wise, exposure of the crystallographic planes and accessibility of
catalyst active sites fitted into the porous structure onto the solid
support is also critical for catalytic activity and selectivity
[73,74]. The higher performance of nanocatalysts is considered
due to the phenomenon of nano-effects, which is believed to result
due to structural, quantum size, and electronic effects [58,59,75].
The wet impregnation method is a widely employed technique
for preparing transition metal nanocatalysts [76]. However, com-
pared to the solution-phase synthesis of metal nanoparticles, the
impregnation method offers poor control over the particle size
and size distribution of resulting metal NPs. Nevertheless, the
method is still prevalent today due to its scope of scalability and
low cost. Other methods for the synthesis of metal nanocatalysts
include coprecipitation, which could be in-situ precipitation of
the metal and the support using sol–gel protocols [77] or using
post-functionalization to deposit the colloidal nanoparticles onto
the support [78] or polymer-assisted method that involves poly-
mer as a template to nucleate and stabilize NPs [79,80]. A decrease
in the size of the catalyst produces a dominant effect on the surface
atoms at edges and corner positions [81,82]. This affects the cat-
alytic activity by creating under-coordinating states on the sur-
faces. It was found that the fractions of metals on surface atoms
having coordination numbers of 4,7,9 in octahedral NPs or 3,6,8
cubic NPs present strong dependences on the size of NPs [83].
The correlation results shown in Fig. 3 illustrate the dependence
of catalytic performance on the size NPs.
The general tendency of increased catalytic activity with the
particle size decreases indicates that the low coordination number
of vertex and edge atoms on the particle surface are active sites for
the Suzuki reaction [85] Fig. 4. Further, a series of well-defined
homopolymer-stabilized Pd colloids with varying metal particle
sizes was utilized to investigate the Heck coupling reaction of ole-
fine and aryl halides [86]. A low reaction rate was obtained when
the Pd precursor was utilized without a polymer, implying the
reaction doesn’t occur through solution-phase catalysis by leached
Pd particles. A quantitative relationship was found between the
initial reaction rates over various stabilized Pd NPS and the number
of low-coordinated (defect) Pd surface atoms calculated using
statistics for face-centered cubic (fcc) cuboctahedron [87]. Initial
reaction rates did not vary, calculated per number of the defect
atoms. The Pd- NPs catalyzed Heck coupling of aryl halides with
olefins was thus so-called to be a structure-sensitive reaction with
low-coordinated atoms as active sites (Fig. 5). These findings agree
with the results for the supported Pd catalyst in the Suzuki cou-
pling reaction [66].

and nonoxides of various sizes and shapes. These may involve no
support materials or may be supported on carbonaceous materials,
polymers, metal oxide, or porous materials such as siliceous
mesocellular foam [50]. The rational design of nanocatalysts is
important to achieve enhanced catalytic activity, chemical and
thermal stability, selectivity, and high efficiency [51]. The tailored
nanomaterials would necessitate tuning their chemical and physi
cal properties as efficient nanocatalysts through particle size,
shape, surface composition, and surface reactivity [52]. It is widely
known that electron transfer occurs between the catalyst surface
and the reactive species in all key steps of the catalytic reactions,
including the reactants adsorption, intermediates diffusion, and
the desorption of the products [53]. Thus, tuning the spatial and
energy distribution of valence electrons at the catalyst surface
would enhance the catalytic efficiency, such as the activation
energy barrier, which in turn is linked to the reactivity and selec-
tivity of the catalysts [54,55]. Based on frontier molecular orbital
theory, adsorption and bonding of reactants on the surface of the
catalyst are dependent upon matching their energy levels to those
of the catalyst surfaces as well as the symmetry and spin state of
the reactant’s molecular or atomic orbitals [56,57]. These proper-
ties of nanomaterials can be achieved/tuned by altering their size,
lattice framework, morphology, quantum size, and electronic
effects from nanopore confinement [58–65]. Likewise, the sup-
port’s size, shape, and composition are critically important in the
design of catalysts [62,63]. In addition, nanocatalysts’ thermal
and chemical stability is also very important since catalysts can
be deactivated because of surface aggregation, leaching, phase
changes, and sintering [64,65].
2.1. Size effect
One of the foremost importance of using nanocatalysts is their
small size because this is directly linked with other parameters
such as high surface area, chemical stability, and reactivity respon-
sible for the enhanced catalytic activities. Therefore, in the past
year, enormous work has been dedicated to nanosized catalysts
to understand the effect of particle size on their catalytic and elec-
tronic properties in numerous transformations, more specifically,
coupling reactions [66,67]. When the size of the NPs decreases,
the ratio of surface to the bulk atoms increases, denoting that more
surface atoms eventually be accessible for the reactions. However,
catalytic activity is not often in direct proportion with the
increased surface area of smaller NPs [68]. The surface of nanocat-
alysts with assorted facets can offer diverse binding force strength
and configuration, which prolong different active sites, steps, and
corners of surface terraces. Therefore, the size and shape of the
NPs significantly affect their catalytic performance [69–76]. Like-
wise, exposure of the crystallographic planes and accessibility of
catalyst active sites fitted into the porous structure onto the solid
support is also critical for catalytic activity and selectivity
[73,74]. The higher performance of nanocatalysts is considered
due to the phenomenon of nano-effects, which is believed to result
due to structural, quantum size, and electronic effects [58,59,75].
The wet impregnation method is a widely employed technique
for preparing transition metal nanocatalysts [76]. However, com-
pared to the solution-phase synthesis of metal nanoparticles, the
impregnation method offers poor control over the particle size
and size distribution of resulting metal NPs. Nevertheless, the
method is still prevalent today due to its scope of scalability and
low cost. Other methods for the synthesis of metal nanocatalysts
include coprecipitation, which could be in-situ precipitation of
the metal and the support using sol–gel protocols [77] or using
post-functionalization to deposit the colloidal nanoparticles onto
the support [78] or polymer-assisted method that involves poly-
mer as a template to nucleate and stabilize NPs [79,80]. A decrease
in the size of the catalyst produces a dominant effect on the surface
atoms at edges and corner positions [81,82]. This affects the cat-
alytic activity by creating under-coordinating states on the sur-
faces. It was found that the fractions of metals on surface atoms
having coordination numbers of 4,7,9 in octahedral NPs or 3,6,8
cubic NPs present strong dependences on the size of NPs [83].
The correlation results shown in Fig. 3 illustrate the dependence
of catalytic performance on the size NPs.
The general tendency of increased catalytic activity with the
particle size decreases indicates that the low coordination number
of vertex and edge atoms on the particle surface are active sites for
the Suzuki reaction [85] Fig. 4. Further, a series of well-defined
homopolymer-stabilized Pd colloids with varying metal particle
sizes was utilized to investigate the Heck coupling reaction of ole-
fine and aryl halides [86]. A low reaction rate was obtained when
the Pd precursor was utilized without a polymer, implying the
reaction doesn’t occur through solution-phase catalysis by leached
Pd particles. A quantitative relationship was found between the
initial reaction rates over various stabilized Pd NPS and the number
of low-coordinated (defect) Pd surface atoms calculated using
statistics for face-centered cubic (fcc) cuboctahedron [87]. Initial
reaction rates did not vary, calculated per number of the defect
atoms. The Pd- NPs catalyzed Heck coupling of aryl halides with
olefins was thus so-called to be a structure-sensitive reaction with
low-coordinated atoms as active sites (Fig. 5). These findings agree
with the results for the supported Pd catalyst in the Suzuki cou-
pling reaction [66].

the metallic state in metal NPs in the range of 1 to 2 nm size
behaves as a molecule [88–95], and the molecule exhibits intrinsi-

2.2. Shape effect
The shape of NPs plays a significant role in the catalytic perfor-
mance of nanocatalysts since NPs with different shapes are synthe-
sized by stabilizing certain facets and allowing the other facets to
grow [108,109]. This strategy could tune the synthesis with
nanocatalysts with exposed active facets and defined atoms on
the corners and edges [110,111]. Packing the atoms in nanocatalyst
surfaces has been found in various shapes such as spherical, cubic,
tetrahedron, octahedron, and truncated octahedron [112–119]. It
has been demonstrated that contrasting atomic arrangements
and interactions of different crystal faces of the same crystal could
have significantly different distributions of valence electrons,
resulting in entirely different molecular adsorption and reactivity
[116,117]. Thus, the controlled design of the metal NPs crystals
with uniform surface facets is necessary for enhanced catalytic
activity and selectivity of the product [118]. These surfaces of
metal NPs with specific shapes are composed of either pure
(100) facets, pure (111), or vicinal surfaces with (730) facets con-
taining denser steps or kinked atoms that result in lowering the
coordination number [119]. Therefore, controlled synthesis of
these shapes provides the prospects to systematically explore the
surface structure to tune the catalytic activity and selectivity of
the catalytic reactions in organic synthesis [84,111]. The low-
index facets such as (100), (110), and (111) of magnetic nanopar-
ticles (MNPs) are preferably exposed due to the lower surface
energy and hence more stability. The variations in structural
aspects stem mainly from the differences in the atomic packing
on the catalyst surfaces [120]. Therefore, the structural variations
between different crystallographic surfaces intrinsically influence
the dissociation, adsorption, coupling, and interactions of the
adsorbed intermediates in the catalytic reactions [84].
A good fraction of the catalysis research was devoted to tailor-
ing metal deposits’ shape on oxide surfaces. One parameter that
controls the particle geometry is the metal-support interaction,
which is typically small for wide-gap oxides, causing the metals
to grow in a 3D fashion [121]. Various approaches were developed
to modify this parameter, for instance, by introducing defects and
species (OH functionalities) into the oxide surface or using polar
oxide terminations with high metal oxide adhesion[122]. Alterna-
tively, electron-transfer processes across the metal oxide interface
may be exploited to alter the growth morphology of metals. This
approach has been demonstrated for thin fil oxides on metal sup-
port first [123]. The shapes of metal nanoparticles, particularly in
wet chemistry synthesis, can be controlled in the twilight zone of
kinetic and thermodynamic control [115]. This is mostly controlled
by the capping ligands, solvents, and temperature by controlling
the nucleation and growth steps [124–130]. El-Sayed et al.
reported that Pt NPs have cubic, tetrahedral, and spherical spira-
cles shapes (Fig. 6). These shapes were controlled by altering the
concentration of capping materials to the concentration of Pt
cations used in the reductive hydrogen method at room tempera-
ture [127]. Later on, the same research group reported the Pt NPs
with various shapes as nanocatalysts for electron transfer reactions
[66,128]. The tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs showed excellent catalytic
activity with the lowest activation energy (14 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>), whereas
cubic-shaped Pt NPs exhibited low catalytic activity, having the
highest activation energy (26.4 kJ mol<sup>1</sup>). The sphericle-shaped
Pt NPs displayed moderate catalytic activity due to exposed facets
and fewer catalytically active atoms on the surface of NPs. Thus,
tetrahedral-shaped Pt NPs exhibiting (111) facets had a large frac-
tion of atoms on the edges and corners of the surface. On the other
hand, cubic-shaped Pt NPs contained (100) facets on the surface
with smaller fractions of atoms on the edges and corners of the
surfaces. Due to these exposed facets and catalytically active atoms
on the surface of tetrahedral NPs, the tetrahedral Pt NPs proved
more active than cubic Pt NPs [128].
The shape dependence of NPs on the reactivity in C C bond for-
mation, e.g., in the Suzuki reaction, has been demonstrated by
Bokhoven et al. [74]. The catalytic activity tends to increase from
spherical to tetrahedral shapes of Pt NPs, which was linked to
the (111) facets of tetrahedral shapes that bear the maximum

2.3. Support materials
In the case of supported metal catalysis, the support materials
have been considered to be inert, and their prime role was to
increase the stability of the metal particles by immobilizing and
dispersing them to improve the active surface area. Later, the Taus-
ter group introduced the term strong metal-support interaction to
elaborate on the unexpected chemisorption properties of
\mathrm { H } _ { 2 }
on
noble metal NPs supported by
\mathrm { T i O } _ { 2 }
[63]. Further, the importance
of the support materials has been explored at a fundamental level,
commonly utilizing model catalysts. In short, the role of the sup-
port materials in catalysis is somewhat more complex and yet to
be explored. Support material can play direct or indirect roles dur-
ing a catalytic transformation. These provide precise defect sites
onto which the metal NPs can be immobilized in the case of meta-
stable particles [131]. In addition, the support can enable the elec-
tronic interactions between metal NPs and provide functionalities
to the nanomaterials, such as acidic sites or basic sites that
improve the stability, activity, and selectivity of the catalyst
Earlier studies have shown that the catalysts inherent activity
and selectivity may vary strongly, contingent on the size of the
metal NPs (>7 nm in diameter). Yet the size is not solely responsi-
ble for varying catalyst efficiencies. The choice of catalyst support
is captious even for materials having the same geometry, for which
mass transport differences can be ruled out [13]. This frequently
turns out that some support materials catalyze unwanted side
transformations, in many cases, the clarification is less frivolous
[134]. In some cases, the NPs catalytic activity decreased upon
recyclability. Therefore, a stabilizer such as a polymer ligand and
surfactant was used to overcome the mentioned issues [135]. A
series of supporting materials such as CNTs [136], colloidal support
[137], silica [137], metal NPs support [138], polymers [139], carbon
[140], and graphene [141] have been reported. On the other hand,
using magnetic NPs as catalyst support could also enable the effec-
tive separation of catalysts from the reaction mixture with the help
of an external magnet [142]. In summary, the nanostructured sup-
port materials hosting the active metal NPs nanocatalysts signifi-
cantly reduce the overall cost, provide simple and scalable
preparation, and easy filtration for efficient recycling [143].

contribution, Liu et al. encapsulated the Pd NPs in a nanoscale
amine-functionalized tubular silica support to form a physically
confined nanocatalyst with a high specific surface area. These
structural features were favourable for good dispersion of Pd
NPs, simple and fast mass transport of reactants, and easy access
of reactants to active sites. Finally, the nanocatalyst was utilized
for the Suzuki coupling reaction with 98 % yield of the coupling
product (Scheme 3) [150].

highly reduced graphene oxide (HRG) as nanocatalyst for the
Suzuki coupling reactions in water (Scheme 5) [153]. The nanocat-

of graphene. The density of the Pd NPs was increased through

the nucleation site for Pd NPs. Likewise, the amino groups also
helped to avoid aggregation and agglomeration of the NPs. The

than HRG-Pd [153]. To investigate the substituent effect, the per

for the Suzuki coupling reaction of bromo, chloro, and iodo ben-
zene and other several types of substituted aryl halides having
both the electron donating groups (EDG) and electron-
withdrawing groups (EWG) with variation of phenyl boronic acid
in aqueous conditions. In the first step, it was investigated that
(Fig. 7) the iodo substituted benzene needed a minimum 5 min

has shown interesting catalytic behavior in the Suzuki coupling

The size and shape of the Pd NPs can be controlled by changing
the reaction condition of the corresponding solution parameters
such as stabilizing ligand, pH, temperature, and time [169]. These
parameters also tune the morphologies of the resulting Pd
nanostructure, e.g., spherical, dendritic, rectangular, and
triangular-shaped Pd [170]. Depending upon morphology, these
nanostructured nanocatalysts can alter the activity and selectivity
of the reaction product. For example, Kamal et al. synthesized the
Pd NPs supported onto carbon spheres. The nanocatalyst was
utilized for the Heck coupling reaction, resulting in significantly
high activity (98 % yield of the product) (Scheme 11) [171]. The
dispersion of the Pd NPs on the carbon surface leads to high
activity and selectivity [172].

Dong and co-workers used a holmium MOF for the Heck and
Suzuki coupling reactions. [Ho(2-TriPP-COO) ] was synthesized
by the treatment of holmium nitrate with 40-(4-car-boxyphenyl)-
2,20:60,20’-terpyridine [182]. The MOF was functionalized with
PdCl (CH CN) . The parent MOF crystallized in a monoclinic space
group with an anion-coordinate HoIIInode linked to six oxygen
atoms and three nitrogen atoms. The SBU had a distorted tricapped
trigonal prismatic geometry (Scheme 15). The MOF was then uti-
lized for the Heck coupling reaction of iodobenzene with methyl
acrylate. As expected, aryl chlorides produced no discernible con-
version. Interestingly, even aryl chlorides produced excellent con-
versions. Pd leaching was found to be 86 ppb [182].
In the Sonogashira reaction, the cross-coupling of aryl or vinyl
halides with terminal alkynes to produce conjugated enynes and
aryl alkynes is also catalyzed by Pd, using copper (I) as a co-
catalyst. The reaction finds many applications in synthesizing nat-
ural products, pharmaceuticals, and other important molecular
frameworks [183–190]. Although Pd-catalyzed Sonogashira
reaction- under homogenous conditions that employ complexes
of Pd(II) salts and phosphine ligands display high activity, it is quite
challenging to recover from reaction mixtures [187]. This makes its
recycling complicated for reuse [187]. Therefore, the heteroge-
neous Pd nanocatalysts, consisting of an active catalytic Pd species
supported on solid support, have been a focus of recent research
interest from the scientific community [114–120].

Polanski et al. developed a novel methodology for a copper-
supported Pd nanocatalyst by transferring nanoparticles to the
target Cu by intermediate carrier SiO [188]. The as-prepared
bimetallic Pd/PdO/Cu nanocatalyst was then used for a series of
Sonogashira reactions. The Pd/PdO/Cu was a highly efficient and
selective catalyst for the reaction between aryl halides and various
terminal acetylenes, giving yields from 63 to 100 % of the corre-
sponding products (Scheme 16) [188]. Ultrasonication was
employed to prevent the aggregation of NPs and retain the cat
alytic activity. Moreover, the recycling of catalysts was facilitated
through catalyst separation from the reaction mixture using cen-
trifugation. In addition, a known amount of phosphine ligand
was used in each round of the cycle to stabilize and inhibit catalyst
deactivation. The performance of the nanocatalysts was proved to
be unchanged within the two repeated cycles (100 % conversions).
The role of Cu was regarded as two folds; (i) as solid support and
(ii) as co-catalyst. The high catalytic activity of the bimetallic
nanocatalysts was linked to the coexistence of PdO species, which
was developed in the Pd/Cu system as revealed by X-ray photo
electron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis [188].

3.2. Platinum nanocatalyst assisted C<sub>A</sub>C bond-forming reactions
Platinum as nanocatalysts for cross-coupling reaction has been
utilized to a limited degree compared to Pd NPs because the oxida-
tive and reductive elimination steps are slower than those of Pd
NPs. However, Narayanan et al. have synthesized tetrahedral-
shaped poly(vinylpyrrolidone) stabilized Pt NPs to catalyze the
Suzuki coupling reaction of aryl halide-like iodobenzene and
phenylboronic acid (Scheme 17) [66]. They concluded that the
morphology of the Pt NPs could be altered from spherical to tetra-
hedral shape through tailoring reaction parameters which, in
return, greatly affect the progress of the Suzuki coupling reaction
[200]. In comparison, spherical shape Pt NPs were found to be
more active than tetrahedral shapes. However, the authors further
investigated that the Pt NPs are not chemically stable under reac-
tion conditions. This leads to a rapid decrease in the catalytic activ-
ity of the nanocatalyst.
Specific engineering of nanomaterials shape, size, surface com-
position, and adsorbed capping ligand is highly important to con-
trol selectivity and catalytic activity. This also differentiates the
colloidally synthesized Pt-based nano-catalysts from normally
used heterogeneous catalysts [201]. Kim et al. developed a block
copolymer with tunable micro and mesoporous structure loaded
with 2 nm size Pt NPs as a nanocatalyst and utilized in ligand
free Suzuki cross-coupling reaction (Scheme 18) [202]. The higher

Tsukuda reported the activity of the colloidal Au NPs (<2 nm)
stabilized by poly(N-vinyl-2-pyrrolidone) (PVP) for the coupling
reaction in water under mild reaction conditions [264]. The dis-
solved oxygen in the water was found to be an important factor
in the reaction. The experimental and theoretical investigation
revealed that the stabilization of the Au NPs using PVP controls
the size of NPs, resulting in enhanced catalytic activity [265,266].
Lambert et al. also reported that the atomically dispersed Au(I)
and Au(II) was found catalytically inert, while the metallic Au(0)
NPs were active and selective towards the Sonogashira coupling
reaction of the phenylacetylene and iodobenzene (Scheme 33).
The author concluded that the metallic Au is active rather than
ionic Au [267].
Metal oxide-supported Au NPs have been synthesized by
deposition–precipitation and incipient wetness impregnation
methods [268–278]. The deposition method leads to the small Au
NPs, while the wetness impregnation method gives larger and
agglomerated particles [271,272]. These NPs were utilized as a cat-
alyst for the Sonogashira coupling reaction of phenylacetylene and
iodobenzene (Scheme 34). The NPs prepared by deposition and
precipitation gave better conversion and selective coupling prod-
ucts 76 % and 75 %, respectively.
The Au NPs exhibited high efficiency in the model C C coupling
reactions. It effectively converted a large variety of functional
groups, including aryl halides to 4-chloro benzoic acid, 4-
chlorobenzaldehyde, and phenylboronic acid, to the corresponding
coupling products in high yield. While testing further scope of the
substrate, the 2-chlorobenzaldehyde showed a relatively lower
yield (76 %) due to steric hindrance and electronic effects of the
substrate present in the aromatic circle environment of aryl
halides. In addition, it was also investigated that the reaction of
phenylboronic acid with 1-chloro-4-vinylbenzene was sluggish,
and after 75 min, the obtained product afforded 75 % yield [254].

3.7. Zinc nanocatalyst-assisted C C bond-forming reactions
Nano-sized zinc (Zn) in the composite used as a nanocatalyst for
the coupling reactions consists mainly of zinc oxide nanomaterials.
The ZnO NPs, when mixed with other metal oxides, exhibited good
catalytic properties for Suzuki cross-coupling reactions under
ligand-free and ambient conditions [280]. The synthesis of ZnO
nanoparticles is accomplished using stoichiometric amounts of
urea and zinc acetate in solution. Then PdCl (3 %) was loaded onto
ZnO NPs using the wet chemistry technique. The catalyst tested for
and efficiently achieved a yield of 97 % for the Suzuki coupling
reactions for the ring-substituted boronic acid and aryl bromides
under ambient reaction conditions (Scheme 37) [280].

4. Conclusion and future perspective
This article demonstrates that the TM-based NPs catalyzed C C
cross-coupling reactions have witnessed phenomenal growth in
the past decade (Fig. 1). The C C coupling transformation finds
its utility in producing biomaterials, fine chemicals, natural prod-
ucts, and medicine [315]. More specifically, the Suzuki, Heck, and
Sonogashira reactions have been widely exploited to generate
diverse structural frameworks and chemical entities. Since homo-
geneous Pd catalysts are far from industrial realism, heterogeneous
metal nanocatalysts have emerged as a promising alternative
owing to their superior catalytic activity, broad substrate scope,
and ease of handling. Moreover, the ease of recovery and reusabil-
ity makes their use a non-hazardous and greener approach, which
is important for sustainability and economic viability. For a higher
catalytic activity, stability, and recyclability of the heterogeneous
metal nanocatalysts system, careful design of the nanocatalysts
size, shape, and morphology is important. Likewise, the architec-
tures of well-defined nanostructured supporting materials have
also made meaningful advancements in the field. Moreover, the
dexterity to integrate the precise nano-sized (1 to 100 nm objects
into the composite nanostructured affords unprecedented oppor-
tunities to generate multiple catalytic interfaces in a single nanos-
tructured catalyst to exploit the synergistic effects between these
catalytic interfaces. Mechanistic understanding of a chemical pro-
cess is equally important. The organic transformations usually fol-
low multistep complex reaction pathways, which need to be fully
understood to understand the role of nanocatalysts. A pedagogical
approach is required to empower the synthetic chemist with the
suitable software and computational chemistry tools needed to

required to shape optimum nanocatalysts [318].
Similarly, the dynamic model for understanding reaction condi
tions in a real reaction environment, such as atomic mobility
within each NPs can also be employed. Finally, new numerical
tools are in high demand to understand the assembly of NPs into
super architectures and their influence on catalytic reactions
[319,320]. Artificial intelligence technology could be a viable solu-
tion to solve grand challenges in organic transformations which
need in-depth chemical intuition. Advanced hardware, enhanced
algorithms, and growing storage capacity would allow scrutinizing
variables beyond the ability of human beings and detection of hid-
den patterns in insignificant and core scale datasheets. The future
of advancement and approaches will ultimately assist the engi-
neering and design of nanocatalysts for the efficient routes (ret-
rosynthesis and prediction of products) with their improvement
(optimization of reaction parameters) to identify new chemical
matter.
